headline: A small town votes to keep Amazon drones out

sources.title: Westborough overwhelmingly votes to restrict commercial drones like Amazon's (Boston.com)
Westborough Votes 510-13 to Ban Amazon Drone Pads and Drop Zones (DroneXL)
Amazon drone delivery plans spark 'serious concerns' (NBC Boston)

chunks.text: On October 19, 2026, more than 500 voters {{turned out}} for a special [[town meeting]] in a small town west of Boston. They voted 510 to 13 for a new [[local rule]]. Its goal is to {{keep Amazon's drones out}}. The rule bans [[launch pads]], where delivery drones {{take off}}. It also bans [[drop zones]], where they leave packages. Amazon, one of the world's biggest companies, wants to {{roll out}} drone delivery from its [[warehouse]] there.

verbs.correct: To be present at an event
verbs.why: Hundreds of fans turn out for every home game. Few people turn out for meetings in the summer. More than 500 voters turned out for a special town meeting.
A tall fence keeps deer out of the garden. The new lock keeps strangers out of the building. The voters' goal is to keep Amazon's drones out of their town.

verbs.correct: To leave the ground and start flying
verbs.wrong: To get power for the battery
verbs.why: Planes take off from this airport every few minutes. The small drone takes off from the roof each morning. The rule bans launch pads, where delivery drones take off.

verbs.correct: To start offering a new service
verbs.wrong: To test a drone near homes
verbs.why: The bank rolls out a new app every few years. Our city rolls out new bike lanes each spring. Amazon wants to roll out drone delivery from its warehouse in the town.

chunks.text: It would be Amazon's first drone delivery [[site]] in New England. The company says its drones would {{drop off}} packages of up to five pounds, usually within an hour of an order. Amazon says the drones' cameras help with [[navigation]] and are not live. It also says the drones are quieter than a delivery truck with its [[engine running]]. The company said it hoped to {{go ahead}} with deliveries before the end of 2026.

verbs.correct: To deliver something to a place
verbs.why: The mail carrier drops off our letters at noon. I drop off my kids at school every morning. Amazon says its drones would drop off packages of up to five pounds.

verbs.correct: To start doing what was planned
verbs.why: If the weather is good, the concert goes ahead. The city goes ahead with the new park when the money arrives. Amazon said it hoped to go ahead with deliveries before the end of 2026.

chunks.text: Many neighbors do not want the drones. About a month before the vote, residents {{set up}} a group to fight the plan. They {{spoke out}} about noise, [[privacy]] and the sight of drones flying [[overhead]]. Some also worry about [[home values]]. In an [[online survey]], 93 percent of those who answered were against the drones. At the meeting, a group member said residents want to protect the town's [[character]] and {{pass it on}} to the [[next generation]].

verbs.why: Parents often set up a group chat for the class. Many students set up a club in their first year. About a month before the vote, residents set up a group to fight the plan.

verbs.correct: To say publicly what you think
verbs.wrong: To sign a letter to a lawmaker
verbs.why: Some workers speak out when their pay is unfair. She always speaks out about safety at work. Residents spoke out about noise, privacy and the sight of drones flying overhead.

verbs.correct: To give something to younger people
verbs.wrong: To sell a home at a high price
verbs.why: Many families pass their homes on to their children. Grandparents pass on old recipes to their grandchildren. One resident said people want to protect the town and pass it on to the next generation.

chunks.text: The vote has [[limits]]. The Federal Aviation Administration controls the sky, so the town cannot stop drones from flying over it. The rule covers only the ground and still allows drones for news and [[emergencies]]. State [[officials]] must {{sign off on}} the rule before it starts. Town leaders are not sure every part will {{hold up}}. A town board has set a November 2 meeting to {{take up}} a separate [[appeal]] from neighbors.

verbs.why: The manager signs off on every new hire. The school board signs off on the budget each June. State officials must sign off on the rule before it starts.

mainIdea.s: Nearly all voters at a meeting in a small Massachusetts town backed a rule against Amazon's drone delivery plan. It covers only the ground, and state officials still need to approve it.
mainIdea.why: Voters approved the rule 510 to 13 to keep Amazon's drones out. It bans places where drones take off, and state officials must sign off on it.

mainIdea.s: After a huge vote, a town near Boston has banned Amazon's delivery drones from flying in its skies. Because of worries about noise and privacy, no drone may pass above any home there now.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the town cannot control the sky. The Federal Aviation Administration does, so the rule only bans places on the ground where drones take off and leave packages.

mainIdea.s: Amazon has begun sending medicine by drone to farms across New England. Company leaders say the new service will cut waiting times for rural families who live far from a drugstore.
mainIdea.why: This is about a town that voted against Amazon's drone plan. Residents spoke out about noise and privacy, and a town board has set a November 2 meeting to take up an appeal.

lines.text: Did you hear about the town that voted against Amazon's drones?
More than 500 people {{turned out}} for a town meeting, and only 13 voted against the new rule.
Wow. What does the rule do?
It bans launch pads where the drones {{take off}}, and places where they {{drop off}} packages.
Why are people so against it? Fast delivery sounds nice.
They want their [[peace and quiet]]. Neighbors {{spoke out}} about noise and privacy.
[[I can't blame them]]. I wouldn't want drones above my house all day.
Some residents even {{set up}} a group to fight the plan.
[[To be fair]], Amazon says the drones are quiet and the cameras aren't live.
True. And the rule can't stop drones from flying above the town. The federal government controls the sky.
It's not clear. State officials have to {{sign off on}} the rule, and town leaders aren't sure every part will {{hold up}}.
So the town doesn't get [[the last word]].
Not yet. A town board has set a November 2 meeting to {{take up}} another appeal.
